note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Acute severe headache for three days, described as blinding and persistent.
- Onset and progression: Sudden onset upon waking three days ago; continuous since then; partial relief with ibuprofen but headache persists.
- Symptoms: Photophobia; sensitivity to light; transient visual phenomena described as “shooting light” or weird vision; no nausea/vomiting reported; no dizziness, weakness, numbness, or speech changes.
- Location and intensity: Pain felt all over with more intensity around the right eye; pain rated 8/10 at worst, down to ~5 with analgesia.
- Impact on function: Difficult to focus and work from home; has taken days off work; night sleep okay, headaches wake him in the morning occasionally.
- Triggers/relievers: Ibuprofen provides partial relief; sleeping normally described; no relief with changing position or coughing noted.
- Recent medical history: Prior headaches in childhood with no ongoing issues; no fever; no recent infections or sinus symptoms.
- Eye/vision history: Recent eye check with no vision changes.
- Medications: Oral contraceptive pill started about one year ago; ibuprofen used for headaches; paracetamol may be used; no other regular medications.
- Allergies: None.
- Social history: Lives alone; does not smoke; consumes alcohol (~3 drinks per week); works from home.
- Red flags discussed: No fever, no vomiting, no focal neurological deficits reported by patient; no cervical stiffness or recent trauma mentioned.

Past Medical History:
- Oral contraceptive pill started ~1 year ago.
- Prior headaches in childhood; no chronic illnesses identified.
- No known drug allergies.
- Ibuprofen and occasional acetaminophen used for headaches.

Physical Examination:
- No physical examination findings documented in the transcript.
- Plan mentions: neurological examination and fundoscopy; BP assessment at follow-up.
- No vitals provided.

Impression:
- Possible migraine-type headache with photophobia and transient visual phenomena; headache ongoing for three days with partial response to NSAID.

Management Plan:
- Medication: Prescribe a medication similar to ibuprofen but stronger for use instead of ibuprofen; allow paracetamol to be taken concurrently. Instruct to take with food.
- Investigations/Examination: Book a full neurological examination and fundoscopy (examine back of eyes); blood pressure to be checked at the appointment.
- Follow-up/Monitoring: If headache settles, appointment can be canceled. If headaches worsen, change in pattern, or new red flags arise, go to A&E for evaluation.
- Contraception consideration: Acknowledge that if migraine features (including flashing lights) persist, the birth control pill may need to be reconsidered, and a change may be required.
- Referrals/Access: Booking through support line for a comprehensive examination; referral to specialist as appropriate after evaluation.

Patient Summary:
- The patient presents with a three-day, persistent, severe headache with photophobia and transient visual phenomena, most noticeable around the right eye. There is partial relief with NSAIDs; work and daily activities are affected. A neurological examination and fundoscopy are planned, and a stronger analgesic regimen plus paracetamol will be started while awaiting the appointment. The possibility of changing the oral contraceptive is discussed if migraine features persist.

Key Takeaways:
- Seek urgent care (A&E) if headache becomes unbearable, worsens rapidly, or new red flags develop (e.g., fever, focal neurologic signs, severe neck stiffness).
- Take the prescribed stronger analgesic with food; you may continue paracetamol as well.
- A neurological exam and fundoscopy are planned; BP will be checked during the visit; consider contraception review if migraine features persist.

Next Steps:
- Schedule and complete a full neurological examination and fundoscopy.
- BP assessment at the appointment.
- Begin prescribed analgesic regimen and paracetamol as needed with food.
- Review oral contraceptive suitability if migraine features persist; potential change if indicated.
- Follow-up arranged via support line; contact sooner if symptoms worsen or new symptoms occur.

- Missing elements: No actual vital signs recorded (BP, temperature, pulse, etc.); no documented physical exam findings; exact drug names, doses, routes, and frequencies for the “stronger” analgesic not specified; no documented allergies beyond “none”; no imaging results ordered; no meds reconciliation beyond pill and OTC analgesics.
- Internal conflicts: None identified in the transcript.
- Transcript quality: Conversation contains procedural planning but lacks concrete exam findings and vitals; some repetition and informal phrasing.
